title: The firewall that wasn't in the way
role: You run a rented VPS for side projects. MongoDB runs in Docker from the official image. The provider offers no outside firewall, so UFW on the box is your only one.

source.label: RealOGs blog: Lessons from a Hack: securing systems properly when using UFW with Docker

brief: You open MongoDB Compass and your databases are gone. In their place is one new database holding a note: send 0.005 BTC within 48 hours or the data gets published.

steps.situation: Someone got in. The container is still running and still reachable.

choices.text: Close the hole first (stop the container), but keep the volume, the container logs and the auth log
choices.why: Stopping the container ends the exposure. The logs tell you how they got in and what else they tried.

choices.text: Pay: the data is worth more than 0.005 BTC
choices.why: Nothing proves the attacker kept a copy, and the hole stays open for the next scanner.

choices.text: Delete everything and redeploy the same compose file
choices.why: You wipe the evidence and recreate the exact same exposure within minutes.

steps.situation: "But UFW denies 27017," you think. You check.
steps.evidence:
$ sudo ufw status
Status: active
To        Action  From
22/tcp    ALLOW   Anywhere
80,443/tcp ALLOW  Anywhere
$ docker ps --format '{{.Names}} {{.Ports}}'
mongo  0.0.0.0:27017->27017/tcp
# from a laptop outside
$ nc -vz 203.0.113.20 27017
Connection to 203.0.113.20 27017 port [tcp/*] succeeded!

choices.text: Believe the outside test, then read the rules Docker added: iptables -t nat -L DOCKER -n
choices.why: `-p 27017:27017` makes Docker write its own iptables rules, and they bypass UFW. `ufw status` only lists UFW's rules.

choices.text: Trust ufw status: they must have come in another way
choices.why: The test from outside just connected. Believe the packet, not the config summary.

choices.text: Add ufw deny 27017 and move on
choices.why: The new rule lands in UFW's chains, which the Docker traffic never meets. Run `nc` again and it still connects.

steps.situation: Only your app on this same host needs the database. How do you publish it?

choices.text: Publish on 127.0.0.1:27017:27017 and set Docker's default bind IP to 127.0.0.1 in daemon.json
choices.why: The author's fix. Docker makes no public rule for a port bound to localhost, and the daemon setting protects the next container you forget.

choices.text: Drop ports: and let the app reach Mongo over the Compose network
choices.why: Also closed, if the app runs in the same Compose project. Fine, but you lose host access for tools like Compass, unless you use a tunnel.

choices.text: Move Mongo to an unusual port, 47017
choices.why: The author also avoids default ports, but only on top of a real fix. Scanners sweep every port; obscurity alone is not a firewall.

steps.situation: The auth log shows another thing: someone has been guessing SSH passwords for days. The provider had password login enabled.
steps.evidence:
$ sudo grep -c 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log
18342
$ sudo sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
passwordauthentication yes

choices.text: Keys only (PasswordAuthentication no), open only 80/443 and SSH, or log in over Tailscale SSH
choices.why: What the author changed. Tailscale SSH runs over a WireGuard tunnel, so no OpenSSH port has to face the internet.

choices.text: Install fail2ban and keep password login
choices.why: It slows the guessing, but a botnet keeps bringing new addresses, and a password stays something that can be guessed.

choices.text: Ignore it: the database was the hole, not SSH
choices.why: Two open doors at once. The next attacker picks the one you left.

debrief.what_happened: The author ran MongoDB in Docker on a VPS, published with `-p 27017:27017`. The provider had no outside firewall, so the author set up UFW and assumed it protected the port. One day the databases in Compass were replaced by a single database with a ransom note (0.005 BTC in 48 hours, or the data would be published). The logs also showed SSH password brute-forcing, because the provider had password login on. The cause: Docker's `-p` opens the port in iptables and bypasses UFW. The fixes in the post: publish to `127.0.0.1`, set the daemon's default IP to 127.0.0.1 in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, avoid default ports, keep only 80/443 and SSH open, turn off SSH passwords, use Tailscale SSH, and use the provider's outside firewall where there is one. The author called the data non-critical; the post does not say whether it came back.
lessons: UFW does not filter ports that Docker publishes: check with a scan from outside.
Bind database ports to 127.0.0.1, or don't publish them at all.
Set a safe default bind IP in daemon.json so a forgotten -p stays local.
Key-only SSH on every internet-facing box, from day one.
